title: Europe Must Step Up to Settle Russia-Ukraine War | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Thomas Graham argues the Abu Dhabi U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks produced no breakthrough but real momentum, and that settlement now hinges on Europe: both the European 'ceasefire first' and Russian 'root causes first' positions are untenable, so the path is a framework agreement on principles of a future European security order plus a commitment to negotiate it after a ceasefire. Europe must urgently decide who represents it amid E3, Nordic and Polish divisions.

themes.theme: Abu Dhabi talks: momentum without breakthrough

insights.claim: The November 2026 trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi produced no breakthrough, but follow-up meetings of envoys Witkoff and Kushner with Putin and Zelenskyy suggest all sides are committed to building on positive momentum.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Diplomatic track is live; watch for incremental ceasefire signals that could move Russia/Ukraine-exposed assets and European defense names.
insights.quote: all sides are committed to trying to build on the positive momentum
insights.locator: The trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: Russia and Ukraine are intensifying their search for an exit from the war despite maximalist Kremlin rhetoric, because the political, economic and demographic costs are mounting rapidly for both sides.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Mounting war costs raise odds of a settlement; Kremlin rhetoric is a poor guide to its actual negotiating intent.
insights.quote: The political, economic, and demographic costs of a bloody war are mounting rapidly for both sides.
insights.locator: That Russia and Ukraine are intensifying

insights.claim: Peace is not close at hand but is now 'thinkable' in a way it has not been since Russia invaded Ukraine nearly five years ago, with diplomacy described as accelerating.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Raise but do not overprice probability of a ceasefire in the near term; positioning for a 'peace trade' remains early.
insights.quote: it is now thinkable in a way it has not been since Russia invaded Ukraine nearly five years ago
insights.locator: None of this should be taken

themes.theme: European security order as the crux of settlement

insights.claim: Key European capitals see the inclusion of Europe's security architecture in the trilateral talks as a major concession to Russia, fearing Moscow will use it to erode NATO's position in eastern Europe, split allies, and prolong the war.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: European resistance is a key source of friction that could slow or derail a deal.
insights.quote: many European leaders saw the agreement to discuss this matter as a major concession to Russia
insights.locator: That the trilateral talks have included

insights.claim: Russia's pre-invasion draft security treaties contained three demands: no further NATO eastward expansion, no deep-strike weapons in NATO states able to reach Russia, and withdrawal of NATO infrastructure to 1997 lines (the NATO-Russia Founding Act).
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: These demands frame what Moscow will seek in any settlement; watch for concessions on deep-strike deployments and NATO posture.
insights.quote: no further NATO expansion eastward, no deployment in NATO states of deep-strike weapons capable of reaching Russian territory
insights.locator: Yet the European position is increasingly untenable

insights.claim: The European insistence that a ceasefire must precede security-order talks is increasingly untenable, because settlement issues such as Ukraine's relationship to NATO, security guarantees and limits on Ukraine's military directly bear on Europe's future security arrangements.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Expect Europe to be pushed off its 'ceasefire first' stance; that shift would be an early indicator of real progress.
insights.quote: Yet the European position is increasingly untenable.
insights.locator: Yet the European position is increasingly untenable

insights.claim: Russia's position that 'root causes' must be resolved before a ceasefire is also untenable, since a new European security order will take considerable time and waiting for it would be 'a recipe for unending war'.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: If Moscow holds to root-causes-first, the war persists; a softening of this condition is a key signal.
insights.quote: Waiting for agreement on a new European security order would be a recipe for unending war
insights.locator: That said, it is also clear

insights.claim: Graham proposes a 'framework agreement': agreement now on the principles and parameters of a future security order plus a credible commitment to negotiate details after a ceasefire, as a compromise between European and Russian sequencing demands.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: A framework deal is the most plausible settlement architecture to watch for in headlines.
insights.locator: The goal in the ongoing negotiations

insights.claim: A settlement could include limits on the size of Ukraine's military capabilities, likely in exchange for limits on Russian military deployments along its border with Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Mutual force limits would shape long-run Ukrainian and European defense procurement demand.
insights.quote: possible limitations on the size of Ukraine’s military capabilities (likely in exchange for limitations on Russia’s military deployments
insights.locator: One does not have to accept

insights.claim: Any settlement will formalize a Russia-Europe frontier from the Barents Sea to the Black Sea, with Belarus, Russia and perhaps Moldova lying in a different geopolitical zone, which would naturally end NATO's eastward expansion.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: An end to NATO enlargement would be a structural concession to Russia that redefines Europe's eastern border risk.
insights.quote: This geographical reality would put a natural end to NATO expansion eastward

insights.claim: The South Caucasus will remain a region contested between Russia and Turkey, among others, even after a Ukraine settlement.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: South Caucasus geopolitical risk (transit corridors, energy routes) persists regardless of a Ukraine deal.
insights.quote: The South Caucasus will remain a region contested between Russia and Turkey

insights.claim: A new Europe-Russia equilibrium would not be cooperative or values-based; rivalry would continue in the Arctic, Black Sea, eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, though commercial and cultural ties could be restored and arms-control and transparency measures could sharply cut war risk under 'competitive coexistence'.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Peace would allow partial restoration of commercial ties but not a return to pre-2022 normalization; sustained European defense spending likely.
insights.locator: A new security order will require

insights.claim: The United States is consulting European capitals, wants Europeans directly in the talks, and supports creation of a Europe-Russia channel on the war and bilateral issues.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: U.S. pushing Europe in reduces risk of a deal imposed over European heads, improving implementability.
insights.locator: How to Walk Through an Open Door

insights.claim: U.S.-Europe tension under the Trump administration has upended Moscow's conviction that Europe was simply a U.S. vassal, leading Russia to recognize it must engage Europe directly.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Transatlantic friction has the second-order effect of raising Europe's independent weight with Moscow.
insights.quote: upended Moscow’s conviction that Europe was simply a U.S. vassal
insights.locator: Russia also understands that it needs

insights.claim: Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on November 13 that Russia is willing to talk with Europe 'if the Europeans truly have someone who is authorized to hold discussions', signaling vague acceptance of European participation.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Russia may exploit European disunity over representation as a lever or delay tactic.
insights.quote: if the Europeans truly have someone who is authorized to hold discussions
insights.locator: Russia also understands that it needs

insights.claim: European unity is fractured: Finnish and Norwegian leaders' outreach to Putin was criticized in some capitals, the E3 (France, Germany, UK) are reportedly building their own channel to Moscow, and Poland fears big powers will negotiate over smaller states' heads.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Intra-European division is a key drag on settlement timing; watch for an agreed European negotiating format.
insights.quote: Poland, among others, fears that these big European powers plan to negotiate arrangements with Russia over the heads of other European states

insights.claim: Europe need not have a single interlocutor: E3 national security advisors could join the multilateral talks while Finnish and Norwegian leaders continue direct talks with Putin, provided roles are clearly delineated and coordinated.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: A multi-channel European format is a plausible near-term outcome to monitor.

insights.claim: The U.S. has played the central role in launching the negotiations and remains critical, but all sides now acknowledge that European participation is indispensable—peace cannot be achieved without Europe.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: European decisions (sanctions, frozen assets, guarantees) become pivotal to any deal's terms and timing.
insights.quote: Peace cannot be achieved without them.
insights.locator: None of this should be taken
